Let me be direct with both of you, because I think the aggressive case and the neutral case are both making the same category error from opposite directions — they're treating a fundamentally excellent business as if fundamental excellence is the same thing as a favorable entry.

Aggressive, I want to start with the thing you keep waving away as a "phantom." You say the controlling shareholder selling 1% is a <5% probability so we shouldn't hedge it. Fine — I'll grant you that. But you've misidentified what the actual tail risk is. The risk isn't that Moutai Group sells. The risk is that on any given morning, the stock gaps down and we cannot get out. That's not a hedge against a shareholder action — that's the structural reality of T+1. And you keep using T+1 as a bull argument: "the first reflex rally runs multiple days, that's a structural edge." The same mechanism that lets a rally run multiple days is the mechanism that locks us into a gap-down overnight. It's symmetrical, and you're only quoting the half that flatters your position. If overnight policy news hits — and this is a policy market, the policy report says so explicitly — we open down, we cannot exit, and our "hard 2x ATR stop at 1381" is a piece of paper that executes at whatever the market gives us, not at 1381. You built a 3% defined-risk trade on a structure where risk is not definable. That's the whole conservative objection in one sentence.

And let's look hard at your asymmetry math, because it's the load-bearing beam of your argument and it's cracked. You say downside to 1381 is -3% and upside to 1485-1510 is 4-6%, so it's a 1.5:1 to 2:1 skew. But where does 1381 come from? It's 2x ATR below spot in a market where ATR is expanding, the stock just broke the 200-day, broke the Bollinger lower band, and the MACD histogram is re-expanding at -10.71. You're pricing risk off a volatility measure while telling us volatility is accelerating. That's not a stop, that's a hope. And the actual downside isn't 1381 — look at the support table in the technical report. Below 1425 there is no近端支撑, the report literally calls it a真空地带, then 1400 psychological, then 1380-1385. A gap through 1400 on T+1 puts you at 1385 before you can do anything, and if 白酒 is in a policy-driven 杀估值, you can queue at limit-down and not fill. The report warns exactly this: limit-down means the buy book is empty and "effectively trapped." You cannot tell me the downside is 3% when the instrument's own structural rules say the downside is "whatever the gap gives you and you can't leave."

Now the policy point, because you accused me of distorting the record and I want to be precise, not defensive. I never said policy was net negative. I said the policy report grades it "中性偏利好（结构性）" with a "轻微正向, +5% to +8%边际影响" and explicitly "下跌有支撑, 上行需基本面与批价验证" — that's not a rocket booster, that's a floor. A floor protects you from catastrophic loss; it does not pay you to buy a broken chart. And you're the one who elided the two negatives. The policy report lists "工作餐不上酒" as a landed 党内法规 and calls it a "短期脉冲情绪冲击." It lists消费税征收环节后移 as a "长期悬顶" risk with the strongest possible grade if it lands. You say we shouldn't build a HOLD on an unproposed policy — correct, and I'm not. I'm building a HOLD on the fact that the bullish catalysts are all "中期趋势, 待验证" while the bearish tape is already printed in volume. The policy put doesn't create upside; it caps downside. Those are different instruments and you're trading them as one.

On valuation, you're doing something I need to flag as an internal contradiction. You cite PE 20x against a "historical 25-35x band" and call it cheap. But the fundamentals report explicitly warns that the PE snapshot is a future-dated function — it's not the 2025-06-13 value, it's a later real-time pull. We do not actually know the PE on the analysis date. And even taking 20x at face value, the report's own framing is that PEG 3.34 already prices the 6% CAGR, meaning the market has already paid for the "quality" and you're not buying a discount, you're buying a fairly-priced excellent asset in a downtrend. Your 25% upside case rests entirely on contract liabilities holding in the 7-8月中报 — which is six to eight weeks away and completely unverified. That's not an asymmetry, that's a bet on an unknown event with a stop that doesn't hold. The conservative position is not "refuse to act on the unknown" — it's "don't size a directional bet around data you admit you don't have."

Neutral, I actually think you're closest to right, but your reasoning needs tightening. You're holding because data is missing. I'd hold for a stronger reason: because the market structure of A-shares makes the cost of being wrong asymmetrically larger than the cost of being late. In a market where I can be gapped through a stop, trapped in a limit-down queue, and cannot exit intraday, the rational posture when the tape is broken and the catalyst calendar is empty until July is to preserve capital and optionality, not to pre-position. Your "wait for three confirmations" is not cowardice — it's the correct response to an instrument that punishes premature entries with non-recoverable losses.

And here's the part that should settle it for the aggressive analyst: his own preferred outcome — the 7-8月中报 showing contract liabilities holding and a PE re-rating — is fully available to us without taking any price risk today. We can wait, watch the 缩量止跌 and the RSI-MACD divergence and the reclaim of 1485, and if the中报 confirms, we buy the re-rating at 1520-1550 with the trend and the fundamentals both verified. Yes, we give up 8-10% of the move. But we also give up the scenario where we're trapped in a gap-down through 1400 with no exit, on a position whose stop was fiction. The conservative framework's entire point is that in this market you don't get paid for being early — you get paid for surviving, and the traders who blow up are the ones who confused a clean float and a great business with a safe entry. The 91.97% gross margin is real. The zero unlocks are real. None of that changes the fact that tomorrow morning we might not be able to sell, and that single structural fact dominates every thesis either of you has built.

So my answer to both: HOLD is correct, but not because we're waiting for a headline. HOLD is correct because in an A-share structure where downside protection mechanisms are crippled, the burden of proof for adding risk sits on the buyer, and that burden has not been met — not by the policy floor, not by the oversold RSI, not by the clean float. The floor caps losses; it doesn't justify a trade. The oversold reading can persist and钝化 for weeks. The clean float protects against supply, not against a broken tape. We hold what we have, we define the triggers precisely, and we let the中报 and the volume tell us when the risk-reward actually flips — because with T+1 and limit-down traps, being the last to confirm is not a flaw, it's the only way to stay in the game.
